weeks.label: Week 9 - Head & Neck Anatomy, Masses & Infections

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Neck
lectures.title: Anatomy of the Neck

blocks.html:
Bones of the neck
  • Axial skeleton: 7 cervical vertebrae
  • Visceral skeleton: hyoid bone plus the laryngeal cartilages (thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage, tracheal rings)

rows: Elevates, retracts and rotates the scapula
Bilateral: flexes the neck forward; unilateral: turns the head to the side
Motor: CN XI; most neck nerves lie deep to it
Phrenic nerve runs on its anterior surface
Bilateral: extends the head; unilateral: flexes the head to the same side
Usually superficial to the posterior scalene; CN XI travels alongside it
blocks.lead: Muscles of the posterior triangle

rows: Elevate the hyoid and larynx in swallowing and speech
Depress the hyoid and larynx to re-establish breathing after a swallow

Mylohyoid: forms the floor of the mouth, elevates the hyoid and mouth floor
Anterior and posterior digastric: depress the mandible, elevate the hyoid
Stylohyoid: retracts the hyoid (tongue retraction), tenses the mouth floor to keep the pharynx open on inspiration

Sternohyoid and omohyoid (superficial layer): depress and retract the hyoid and larynx; omohyoid (two bellies on an intermediate tendon) also tenses the carotid sheath to keep IJV pressure low
Sternothyroid: depresses the larynx; alone, pulls the thyroid lamina from the hyoid to open the laryngeal inlet in forced inspiration
Thyrohyoid: the exception, can depress the hyoid or elevate the thyroid cartilage
blocks.lead: Muscles of the anterior triangle

blocks.html:
Arteries of the neck
  • Common carotid: left from the aortic arch, right from the brachiocephalic trunk
  • Internal carotid: enters the skull through the carotid canal to supply the brain; no branches outside the skull
  • External carotid: stays outside the skull with many branches ("Some Attendings Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students")
    • Superior thyroid: first (most inferior) branch
    • Ascending pharyngeal: smallest, the only medial branch
    • Lingual: tongue
    • Facial: muscles and skin of the face
    • Occipital: back of the head
    • Posterior auricular: behind the ear
    • Maxillary: major supply to deep face, nose and palate
    • Superficial temporal: terminal branch, the temple pulse
  • Subclavian branches in the neck
    • Vertebral: runs through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae and enters the skull through the foramen magnum; no branches outside the skull
    • Thyrocervical trunk: many neck branches, including the inferior thyroid artery
Veins of the neck
  • External jugular: superficial head and neck → subclavian vein
  • Internal jugular: brain and skull → brachiocephalic vein

rows: Largest endocrine gland; between the thyroid cartilage and the 5th tracheal ring, C5-T1; deep to the infrahyoid muscles, wrapping the anterior and lateral trachea and the lateral esophagus

Superior thyroid a. (external carotid)
Inferior thyroid a. (subclavian, via the thyrocervical trunk)

Superior thyroid v. → internal jugular vein
Inferior thyroid v. → brachiocephalic vein
blocks.lead: Thyroid gland: highly vascular

rows: Emerges along the posterior border of SCM
Skin of the neck, posterior scalp, shoulders, part of the face
Loops around the IJV, upper root runs with CN XII; embedded in the carotid sheath, hard to find
Anterior rami in the lower neck
In the carotid sheath, between the IJV and the internal/common carotid
Sensory and motor to the larynx and pharynx; parasympathetic to thoracic and gut viscera
Crosses the posterior triangle alongside levator scapulae
Deep to the posterior digastric into the oral cavity
Either side of the vertebral column, deep to the carotid sheath; superior, middle and inferior cervical ganglia
Sympathetic fibres to the head and neck
blocks.lead: Nerves of the neck: spinal nerves C1-C8 are mixed (motor + sensory); most nerves lie deep to SCM

rows: The whole neck; splits around trapezius, SCM, parotid and submandibular glands (a swollen, infected submandibular gland is painful because it is confined)
Vertebral column and its surrounding muscles
Common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve
blocks.lead: Fascial layers of the neck: they limit and direct the spread of infection or cancer
Potential spaces: gaps between the fascial layers that infection can track through

blocks.html:
Carotid triangle
  • Boundaries: superior SCM (posterior), posterior digastric (superior), superior belly of omohyoid (inferior)
  • Contents: internal and external carotid arteries, internal jugular vein, sympathetic trunk, vagus, hypoglossal and spinal accessory nerves, ansa cervicalis
  • Carotid sinus: baroreceptors at the carotid bifurcation that sense stretch (baroreceptor reflex); innervated by a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Lymphatics
  • Head lymphatics drain to neck nodes that follow the internal jugular vein
  • They empty at the IJV-subclavian junction: thoracic duct on the left, right lymphatic duct on the right

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Vagus in carotid sheath → superior laryngeal n.: external = motor to cricothyroid (injury → weak, tired voice / ↓ pitch); internal = sensory to superior larynx (cough reflex)
  • Recurrent laryngeal n. = motor to most laryngeal muscles → injury = hoarseness (unilateral), loss of voice (bilateral)
  • Right RLN loops the subclavian a.; left RLN loops the aortic arch

lectures.framing: The neck is a transitional conduit between the head, thorax and upper limbs. This page walks it layer by layer: bones, the muscles of the posterior and anterior triangles, the arteries and veins, the thyroid and its blood supply, the nerves, and finally the fascial planes and potential spaces that steer the spread of infection and cancer.
lectures.keypoints: The internal carotid and vertebral arteries give no branches outside the skull; the external carotid gives eight (Some Attendings Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students), the superior thyroid first. Thyroid: superior thyroid a. from the external carotid, inferior thyroid a. from the subclavian (thyrocervical trunk). Phrenic nerve C3-C5 runs on the anterior scalene. The carotid sheath holds the common/internal carotid, IJV and vagus. Retropharyngeal space → superior mediastinum; alar "danger" space → posterior mediastinum. Suprahyoids elevate the hyoid, infrahyoids (strap muscles, ansa cervicalis) depress it.

lectures.name: Integrative Upper Respiratory Tract and GI Tract Anatomy
lectures.title: Integrative Upper Respiratory Tract and GI Tract Anatomy
lectures.framing: The pharynx is the shared passage for air and food, so this page follows a bolus from front to back: the oral cavity and tongue, the salivary glands, the three parts of the pharynx and their tonsils, the pharyngeal and palatal muscles, then their blood and nerve supply and the esophagus. The organising idea is which nerve does what, because the tongue and pharynx are built from several developmental sources, each bringing its own nerve.
lectures.keypoints: Tongue: anterior 2/3 general sensation = lingual n. (V3), taste = facial n. (VII, carried by the lingual); posterior 1/3 sensation and taste = CN IX; all tongue muscles = CN XII except palatoglossus (CN X). Pharynx and palate motor = CN X, except stylopharyngeus (CN IX) and tensor palati (V3). Tensor palati is the key soft palate muscle. Sensory: V2 nasopharynx and palate, IX oropharynx, X larynx. Foramen cecum = thyroid remnant. Parotid (Stensen's) most likely to have a mass, least likely malignant; sublingual the reverse. Palatine tonsils sit between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.

blocks.html:
Oral cavity
  • Oral cavity proper: between the upper and lower dental arcades, anterior to the palatoglossal arch (the divider from the pharynx)
  • Vestibule: between the teeth and gums and the lips and cheeks
Tongue
  • Body (anterior 2/3): mobile, in the oral cavity
  • Root (posterior 1/3): fixed, in the pharynx
  • Terminal sulcus: V-shaped line dividing body from root, lined by the circumvallate papillae
  • Foramen cecum: blind pit at the apex of the sulcus, remnant of thyroid development

rows: Bulk of the tongue; depresses the centre, creates a furrow, protrudes the tongue
From the styloid process; retracts and elevates the tongue
Quadrangular; depresses the sides of the tongue; landmark for the lingual nerve, submandibular duct and CN XII (lateral) and lingual artery (medial)
Elevates the back of the tongue or pulls down the soft palate, narrowing the isthmus of fauces; innervated like the pharynx (CN X)
Superior longitudinal (retracts, broadens, raises the tip); inferior longitudinal (retracts, broadens, lowers the tip); vertical (broadens and elongates); transverse (narrows and elongates)
Mylohyoid (forms the floor, moves the tongue in chewing and speech); geniohyoid (supports the tongue, controls the hyoid)
blocks.lead: Muscles of the tongue

rows: General sensation; carries the facial nerve's taste fibres and its parasympathetics to the submandibular ganglion, submandibular and sublingual glands
blocks.lead: Innervation of the tongue: blood supply is the lingual artery (external carotid), with facial and maxillary arteries supplying the rest of the mouth and teeth

rows: Stensen's (parotid) duct, opens near the upper 2nd molar
Most likely to have a mass, least likely malignant
Wharton's duct runs along the floor of the mouth, opens lateral to the frenulum; gland wraps around mylohyoid
Several small sublingual ducts; the largest (Bartholin's) joins Wharton's duct
Least likely to have a mass, most likely malignant if it does
blocks.lead: Salivary glands: three pairs that moisten the mucosa and lubricate chewing

blocks.html:
Relationships in the floor of the mouth
  • On the lateral side of hyoglossus: the lingual nerve and submandibular duct; the lingual nerve loops under and around the duct as it runs forward
  • CN XII runs parallel to and below the lingual nerve, also lateral to hyoglossus
  • The lingual artery runs with CN XII but on the medial side of hyoglossus

rows: Behind the nasal cavity; sphenoid above, soft palate below

Pharyngeal tonsils (adenoids): enlarge and block the airway in adenoid hypertrophy
Pharyngotympanic (Eustachian) tube: equalizes middle ear pressure
Soft palate above, epiglottic vallecula below; palatoglossal arch in front

Palatoglossal arch (isthmus of fauces; palatoglossus)
Palatine tonsils just behind it
Palatopharyngeal arch (palatopharyngeus; closes off the nasopharynx in swallowing)
Lingual tonsils on the root of the tongue
Vallecula above, esophageal opening at the cricoid cartilage below
Laryngeal inlet (epiglottis, quadrate membrane, arytenoids); true and false vocal folds
blocks.lead: Pharynx: attaches to the skull base between the medial pterygoid plates and carotid canal; superior constrictor attaches at the pharyngeal tubercle

rows: Nasopharynx, around the auditory tube opening
Oropharynx, between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
blocks.lead: Waldeyer's ring: first line of defence against organisms entering through the nose and mouth; prominent in childhood, shrink with age, and common sites of infection

blocks.html:
Pharyngeal muscles
  • Constrictors (superior, middle, inferior): 3 paired semicircular muscles stacked like cups; peristalsis in swallowing
  • Longitudinal muscles: lift the larynx and pharynx in speech and swallowing
    • Stylopharyngeus: enters between the superior and middle constrictors; landmark for the constrictors and the pharyngeal plexus (on the middle constrictor); CN IX travels along it
    • Salpingopharyngeus: from near the auditory tube opening, blends into the constrictors
    • Palatopharyngeus: within the palatopharyngeal arch

rows: Tenses the soft palate; most important, it anchors the other palatal muscles
Elevates the soft palate to seal the nasopharynx in swallowing
Depresses the soft palate after swallowing
Depresses the soft palate after swallowing
blocks.lead: Palate: the hard palate (bone, anterior) and soft palate (muscle, posterior) separate the oral and nasal cavities; without palatal elevation food would come out of the nose

blocks.html:
Blood supply of the pharynx and palate
  • All from external carotid branches: superior thyroid (laryngopharynx), ascending pharyngeal (naso- and oropharynx), facial (part of the oropharynx)
  • Maxillary a.: descending palatine → greater palatine (posterior hard palate) and lesser palatine (soft palate); sphenopalatine (a direct maxillary branch) reaches the anterior hard palate through the nose
  • Veins (pterygoid plexus, common facial, inferior thyroid, maxillary) all end in the internal jugular vein

rows: Most muscles of the pharynx and palate
blocks.lead: Pharyngeal plexus (CN X, CN IX and sympathetics from the superior cervical ganglion; lies on the middle constrictor)

blocks.html:
Esophagus
  • Fibromuscular tube from about C6 to T10; moves food to the stomach by peristalsis
  • Mucosa: deeply folded stratified squamous epithelium, allowing distension
  • Submucosa: loose connective tissue rich in elastin plus seromucous glands for lubrication
  • Muscularis: inner circular and outer longitudinal layers

lectures.name: Thyroid Masses
lectures.title: Thyroid Masses

blocks.html:
Thyroid nodules
  • Incidence = 50%, females > males; ↑ with age and low iodine intake
  • Only 5% are malignant; 99% are asymptomatic
  • Think of everything in the area: thyroid, parathyroids, lymph nodes, skin, soft tissue
Thyroid axis

TRH (hypothalamus) → TSH (anterior pituitary) → T3 + T4 → ↑ metabolic rate, ↑ sympathetic activity, steroid hormone release, erythropoiesis

rows: Bradycardia, diastolic hypertension, cold intolerance, dry skin, coarse hair, brittle nails
Tachycardia, systolic hypertension, heat intolerance, anxiety, insomnia, weight loss

Differentiated carcinoma (papillary, follicular)
Poorly differentiated carcinoma
Medullary carcinoma
blocks.lead: Differential of a thyroid mass: inflammatory/infectious (thyroiditis, rare abscess), autoimmune (Graves, Hashimoto's), metabolic (iodine deficiency, toxic multinodular goitre), neoplasm, cyst

rows: Toxic/non-toxic multinodular goitre, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, cysts, follicular adenoma
Well differentiated, slow growing, localized; lymphatic spread; ↑ thyroglobulin
Lymphoma, metastases from other primaries, sarcoma
blocks.lead: Thyroid neoplasms

blocks.html:
History and physical
  • Ask about three things: risk of cancer (family history, speed of growth), local effects (feel of the mass, stridor, dysphagia) and hormonal effects (thyrotoxicosis)
  • Risk factors: child or younger patient, male, 1st-degree relative, neck irradiation (including total body irradiation for BMT, Chernobyl/Fukushima), Filipino ancestry
  • Symptoms: dysphagia, hoarseness (vocal cord paralysis), stridor, rapid growth, voice change
  • Signs
    • Benign: soft, smooth, small, can be tender
    • Malignant: hard, fixed, solitary, > 4 cm, does not move with swallowing, grows rapidly, suspicious cervical nodes

Investigation pathway
  1. TSH first (best screen for function)
  2. Low TSH → radioactive iodine uptake scan
    • Hot (high uptake, hyperfunctioning) = benign, never cancer: no further work-up, treat the hyperthyroidism
    • Cold → ultrasound
  3. Normal/high TSH or cold nodule → ultrasound, scored by ACR TI-RADS (composition, echogenicity, shape, margin, echogenic foci)
    • Malignant features: taller than wide, hypoechoic, microcalcifications, irregular borders, lymphadenopathy
  4. Refer for FNAB if:
    • Hypoechoic and solid > 1 cm ± suspicious features
    • Iso-/hyperechoic or partially cystic without suspicious features > 1.5 cm
    • Spongiform or complex cystic > 2 cm
  5. FNA is the best biopsy for a thyroid or neck mass; the report gives adequacy, diagnosis (malignancy risk) and observations, classed by the Bethesda system

blocks.title: FNA limit
blocks.html: Follicular adenoma (benign) and follicular carcinoma cannot be told apart on FNA. This is why a non-functioning Bethesda IV nodule goes to diagnostic hemithyroidectomy.

rows: AUS (atypia of undetermined significance) or FLUS (follicular lesion of undetermined significance)
Follicular neoplasm or suspicious for follicular neoplasm
If TSH is low, consider radionuclide scan and molecular testing (non-functioning = diagnostic hemithyroidectomy)
Malignant: papillary, follicular, medullary, anaplastic, poorly differentiated, metastatic to thyroid, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, SQCCA
blocks.lead: Bethesda system: total thyroidectomy means supplemental thyroid hormone (levothyroxine) for life.

rows: Clinical follow-up; no repeat ultrasound or biopsy unless the nodule changes
blocks.lead: Putting TI-RADS and Bethesda together

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Nodules very common, more common in females; only 10-15% of palpable nodules malignant (Roth)
  • Work-up: TSH first → low TSH → RAI scan (hot nodule = benign, treat hyperthyroidism); normal/high → U/S (TI-RADS) → FNAB (Bethesda); thyroglobulin not recommended
  • Cancer risk: child, male, 1st-degree FHx, neck radiation; sx dysphagia, hoarseness, stridor, rapid growth; signs firm/fixed mass, suspicious LN
  • Papillary = most common thyroid ca (>85%), best prognosis
  • Post-thyroidectomy voice: RLN injury → unilateral hoarseness, bilateral airway obstruction; SLN injury → loss of pitch control

lectures.framing: Thyroid nodules are common and rarely malignant, so the job is to find the few that need surgery without over-investigating the rest. The work-up follows one pathway: TSH decides the first test, ultrasound features (TI-RADS) decide whether to biopsy, and FNA cytology (Bethesda) decides management. The page covers the hormone basics, the neoplasm types, risk factors, the pathway, and how TI-RADS and Bethesda combine into a plan.
lectures.keypoints: Nodules in 50%, only 5% malignant, females > males. TSH first: low TSH → radioactive iodine scan; a hot nodule is benign (treat hyperthyroidism); normal/high TSH or cold nodule → ultrasound. Suspicious US: taller than wide, hypoechoic, microcalcifications, irregular borders. Papillary is most common (lymphatic spread), follicular spreads hematogenously, medullary raises calcitonin (C cells), anaplastic and lymphoma are urgent. FNA cannot tell follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma. Red flags: child, male, FHx, neck radiation; hoarseness, stridor, rapid growth, hard fixed mass.

lectures.name: Adult Head & Neck Masses
lectures.title: Adult Head & Neck Masses

blocks.html:
Normal structures that feel like masses
  • Submandibular gland (most common; prominent in some people)
  • C2 transverse process (hard)
  • Carotid bulb (carotid sinus, at the bifurcation)
  • Sternocleidomastoid, hyoid bone
  • Cervical rib: congenital overgrowth of a transverse process (usually C7), 0.5-1% of people
Differential (CITTENS)

Congenital, infectious, toxins, trauma, endocrine, neoplasms, systemic. First step: is the mass midline or lateral?

rows:
Thyroid (90%): goitre, tumour, thyroglossal duct cyst
Other (10%): lymph node, dermoid cyst (submental, present at birth, all germ layers, grows so is excised), lymphatic malformation, superficial mass

Infection: reactive nodes (react to an infection elsewhere) vs suppurative lymphadenitis (the node itself is infected; overlying skin red and inflamed)
Congenital: second branchial cleft cyst, thyroglossal duct cyst, lymphatic malformations
Neoplasms: cancers
Trauma/toxins: injection drug use in the neck

blocks.html:
Rules for lateral neck masses
  • Rule of 7s: 7 days = infection; 7 weeks-7 months = neoplasm; 7 years = congenital
  • 80% rule: 80% neoplastic → 80% of those malignant → 80% metastatic (to cervical nodes) → 80% from a head and neck primary (above the clavicles)
  • Age rule: < 16 years = congenital; > 40 years = neoplastic
  • Age + 80% rule: in an elderly patient, a lateral neck mass is cancer until proven otherwise

Work-up
  • Hx: onset, duration, growth, pain; recent H&N infections; exposures (animals, travel, TB); skin cancer, dental work, smoking/EtOH, radiation, FHx, immunodeficiency, age
  • PEx: size, mobility, tenderness, fluctuance, consistency, solitary vs generalized nodes, overlying skin; look for the primary (nasal cavity, nasopharynx, oral cavity, oropharynx, ear canal, scalp, thyroid, salivary glands) and palpate where possible; cervical node exam: lower lymph node = worse
  • Ix
    • Labs: CBC + diff (↑ WBC suggests infection), monospot (EBV), serology by exposure
    • Ultrasound: good first image (cystic masses, nodes)
    • FNAB: culture and sensitivity if infectious, cytology if neoplastic
    • Nasal endoscopy (ENT referral); CT/MRI (abscess, tumour, vascular lesion, extent, nodes)
    • Open neck biopsy: persistent nodes or suspected lymphoma with no obvious primary
    • Panendoscopy under GA: find the primary site

rows: Stensen's duct: buccal mucosa opposite the upper 2nd molar
Wharton's duct: papilla on either side of the frenulum
Small sublingual ducts, the largest joining Wharton's
blocks.lead: Salivary glands: the smaller the gland, the more likely a tumour is malignant. About 1.5 L of saliva a day (99.5% water), under parasympathetic control; it lubricates, digests, protects (IgA, lysozyme, lactoferrin) and mediates taste.

rows: ↑ salivary viscosity → stagnation → salts precipitate → obstruction

Salivary stasis and retrograde migration of bacteria (S. aureus, viridans strep, H. influenzae, E. coli) or viruses (HIV, mumps, coxsackie, influenza)
Risk: dehydration, post-surgery, radiation/chemo, Sjögren's
Pain and swelling, salivary colic worse with meals
Pain, swelling, induration, warmth, tenderness, pus at the duct orifice
Palpation, sialography (submandibular radiopaque, parotid radiolucent), ultrasound, CT, sialendoscopy (rare)
Fistula, acute suppurative sialadenitis, ductal stricture
Gland massage, bimanual stone expression, hydration, sialagogues (sour foods), antibiotics; surgery for complications
Gland massage, warm compress, hydration, sialagogues, antibiotics (IV if needed); no better in 3 days → look for complications
blocks.lead: Salivary gland disorders: also functional problems: hypersecretion (rare), drooling (poor oral-motor coordination), dry mouth (common: drugs such as beta-blockers, chemo, psychotropics; Sjögren's; dehydration; radiation); treat the cause

blocks.html:
Salivary gland tumours
  • Risk factors: radiation (7-30 year latency); NOT associated with smoking/EtOH, EXCEPT Warthin's tumour
  • Usually a painless lump; red flags: abnormal growth, facial nerve weakness (CN VII runs through the parotid), pain, overlying skin changes, hard fixed mass, neck nodes
  • Ix: full Hx and PEx including skin cancer inspection and facial nerve assessment; ultrasound, CT, FNAB
  • Tx: every salivary mass is excised (diagnostic and therapeutic; benign masses keep growing and can transform): complete resection, preserve the facial nerve; superficial parotidectomy (lobe above the nerve) or total parotidectomy (above and below); radiation for cancers
  • Benign neoplastic: pleomorphic adenoma (superficial lobe), Warthin's tumour (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum, the smoking-linked one), other adenomas
  • Benign non-neoplastic: branchial cleft cyst, salivary cysts, inflammation (stone, infection)
  • Malignant: primary (high or low grade), secondary (skin cancer over the parotid invading it), lymphoma

Head and neck cancers
  • Skin cancer is the most common H&N cancer; non-melanoma skin cancer affects 1 in 6 Canadians; melanoma rising 2% a year
  • H&N cancer patients have the poorest health-related quality of life of all cancer patients (talking, eating, breathing, appearance)
  • Squamous cell carcinoma: mucosal lining of the nose, paranasal sinuses, oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, esophagus, ear; 4 main sites: oral cavity, oropharynx, larynx/laryngopharynx, nasopharynx
  • Risk factors: smoking/EtOH, HPV-16 (oropharyngeal; tonsils, base of tongue), EBV (nasopharyngeal), sun, previous cancers, radiation, FHx, wood dust/heavy metals (sinonasal), immunosuppression
  • Oropharyngeal carcinoma is the fastest-rising cancer in North American non-smokers (+5%/year)

rows: Younger, healthy, better educated, higher SES, more sexual partners
Older, poor health and oral hygiene
blocks.lead: HPV-positive vs HPV-negative SCC: HPV-16 causes about 90% of HPV-related H&N SCC

blocks.html:
Red flags by region
  • Ear: persistent otalgia (referred, normal ear exam), unilateral otitis media with effusion, hearing loss, aural fullness, pulsatile tinnitus
  • Nose / sinus / nasopharynx: recurrent epistaxis, unilateral nasal obstruction, persistent rhinorrhea or sinusitis
  • Mouth / pharynx: sore throat > 3 weeks, odynophagia, dysphagia, trismus, non-healing ulcers, halitosis, numbness over teeth, hemoptysis; leukoplakia (white) and erythroplasia (red) are premalignant
  • Larynx: hoarseness and throat pain > 3 weeks, stridor
  • Neuro: look for asymmetry (facial weakness, cranial nerve palsy, diplopia), mental status change
  • Constitutional: night sweats, fever, weight loss
Investigation and treatment
  • Ix: flexible endoscopy, FNAB, tissue biopsy, CT/MRI, CT chest (staging), panendoscopy (primary site)
  • Early disease: single modality (surgery or radiation); advanced: surgery + radiation, or chemotherapy + radiation
  • By site: oral cavity → surgery ± post-op radiation; oropharynx → radiation + chemo; larynx → radiation (advanced: surgery + radiation); neck nodes → surgery ± radiation

Hoarseness: work-up
  • Hx: age, occupation, voice use/abuse, character of the hoarseness, risk factors (cancer, trauma, surgery), other ENT issues, systemic symptoms (weight loss, fever, sore throat)
  • PEx: look, listen, feel

rows: Nodule, Reinke's edema, muscle tension dysphonia
Watch and wait, speech therapy, medialization, injection laryngoplasty
blocks.lead: Hoarseness: red flags are persistent (> 2 weeks) or progressive, positive risk factors, associated symptoms (dysphagia, otalgia, stridor)

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Midline mass = thyroid thing 90% of the time; other 10%: LN, dermoid cyst, lymphatic malformation
  • Rule of 7s: 7 d infection · 7 wk-7 mo neoplasm · 7 y congenital
  • 80% rule: neoplastic → malignant → metastatic → H&N primary; + age rule → elderly lateral neck mass = cancer until proven otherwise
  • Reactive LN (reacts TO infection) vs suppurative lymphadenitis (node itself infected)
  • Stones: submandibular most common; 90% submandibular radiopaque, 90% parotid radiolucent; pain + swelling worse with meals
  • Acute sialadenitis: S. aureus, 25% bilateral; massage, warm compress, hydration, sialagogues, abx; no improvement in 3 d → assess for complications
  • Salivary tumours >80% parotid; smaller gland = greater chance of cancer (parotid 25%, SMG 50%, others 75%); risk = radiation, not smoking/EtOH except Warthin's
  • Salivary tumour red flags: facial nerve weakness, pain, skin changes, hard fixed mass, neck nodes
  • Every salivary gland mass → surgical excision, even if benign; cancers → post-op RT
  • SCC: HPV+ younger, healthier, non-smoker → better prognosis; HPV− older, smoker/drinker → poor
  • Leukoplakia (white) + erythroplasia (red) = premalignant
  • Tx by site: oral cavity surgery ± post-op RT · oropharynx RT + chemo · larynx RT (advanced → surgery + RT) · neck surgery ± RT

lectures.framing: The key to a neck mass is knowing what lives in the neck and what can spread to neck nodes. The page first rules out normal structures, then splits abnormal masses into midline (mostly thyroid) and lateral (infection, congenital, neoplasm) and applies the rule of 7s, the age rule and the 80% rule. It then covers the work-up, the salivary glands (stones, infection, tumours), squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck, and hoarseness.
lectures.keypoints: Midline mass = thyroid 90%. Rule of 7s: 7 days infection, 7 weeks-7 months neoplasm, 7 years congenital. 80% rule + age > 40 → a lateral neck mass in an older adult is cancer until proven otherwise; lower nodes = worse. Stones: submandibular, pain worse with meals. Sialadenitis: S. aureus; reassess at 3 days. Salivary tumours: the smaller the gland, the more likely malignant; not linked to smoking except Warthin's; facial nerve weakness is the red flag; every mass is excised. SCC: HPV-16 → oropharynx (tonsil, tongue base), younger non-smokers, better prognosis; leukoplakia and erythroplasia are premalignant. Hoarseness > 2-3 weeks needs a look at the larynx.

lectures.name: Infections of the Head and Neck
lectures.title: Infections of the Head and Neck

rows: Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA, MRSA), group A streptococcus (cause neck infections, e.g. with injection drug use)
Streptococcus spp. (viridans group); anaerobes Peptostreptococcus (gram +), Fusobacterium (gram −), Parvimonas micra (gram +); occasionally yeast
The "pneumonia of the face": S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, S. aureus
blocks.lead: Head and neck infections: usual organisms

blocks.html:
Choosing antibiotics
  • Cover gram-positives (S. aureus, S. pyogenes) and anaerobes (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas)
  • Ceftriaxone + metronidazole (Flagyl), or amoxicillin-clavulanate, is usually enough
  • Piperacillin-tazobactam only if at risk of Pseudomonas

blocks.alt: Map of organisms by gram stain and oxygen requirement
blocks.cap: Organism map: gram-positives left, gram-negatives right, aerobes above, anaerobes below; mouth anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus) sit left, lower GI anaerobes (B. fragilis) right, and resistance rises toward MRSA and Pseudomonas at the edges.

blocks.alt: Antibiotic coverage overlaid on the organism map
blocks.cap: The same map overlaid with antibiotic coverage: ceftriaxone covers aerobes on both sides but not anaerobes, which is why metronidazole (Flagyl) is added for oral flora; carbapenems are widest and vancomycin covers gram-positives only.
Gram-positive tree: cocci split by catalase (staph vs strep/enterococcus), staph by coagulase (S. aureus positive), and strep by hemolysis (viridans and S. pneumoniae alpha, group A strep beta).

Gram-negative tree: Moraxella among the aerobic cocci, Fusobacterium among the anaerobic bacilli, H. influenzae as a no-growth bacillus on sheep blood agar, and Pseudomonas on the oxidase-negative, non-lactose-fermenter branch as drawn.

blocks.html:
Common neck infections
  • Pharyngitis: mostly viral (rhinovirus, coronaviruses, influenza, parainfluenza, EBV, CMV); bacterial = group A strep; also consider gonorrhea and chlamydia
  • Periodontal disease / tooth abscess: overgrowth of normal oral flora
No longer common (vaccination)
  • Epiglottitis (Hib): epiglottic swelling → acute airway obstruction; an emergency
  • Diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae): grey pharyngeal membrane, respiratory compromise, myocarditis

rows: Entirely within the tonsillar pillar, or removed
blocks.lead: Tonsillitis: grading tonsil size

blocks.html:
Tonsillitis: work-up
  • Hx: tonsil size, redness, exudate, lymphadenopathy, exposures (previous infections and swabs), vaccinations
  • PEx: trismus, reduced ROM, tonsil grade, size/exudate/cervical nodes
  • Red flags: peritonsillar swelling + uvula deviation (peritonsillar abscess → incision and drainage); trismus + restricted neck range (deep neck infection); progressive symptoms, fever, prior antibiotics; always consider the airway
  • Ix: CBC + diff, serology, tumour markers, TSH; CXR, CT, ultrasound
  • Tx: watch and wait (48-72 h); antibiotics (amoxicillin + clavulanic acid); incision and drainage; tonsillectomy (bacterial)
Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy
  • 7 episodes in 1 year, 5/year for 2 years, or 3/year for 3 years
  • Other indications: obstructive sleep apnea, malignancy, ADD, peritonsillar abscess, tonsil stones, chronic tonsillitis, halitosis

rows: Infection tracking through the fascial spaces
Infectious thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein
Angio-invasive fungal infection (rhinocerebral), very high mortality; respiratory or skin presentation
Spread from a bacterial focus: teeth, tonsils, parotid, deep cervical nodes, middle ear, sinuses (oral flora)
Mucorales fungi; risk: severe immunocompromise, diabetes (DKA), steroids, iron chelator (deferoxamine)
Pharyngitis, then fever about 1 week later, chills, rigors, toxic appearance; induration along the IJV
Rapid-onset fever, sinus pain, headache, nasal discharge; necrotic palate
Ceftriaxone + metronidazole; + vancomycin if MRSA risk (colonized, injection drug use); + pip-tazo for Pseudomonas risk (immunocompromised, healthcare-associated); incision and drainage
Airway compromise; spread to the mediastinum
blocks.lead: Rare but dangerous neck infections

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Normal flora: skin S. aureus, GAS; mouth viridans strep + anaerobes (± yeast)
  • Not normal flora: otitis externa → Pseudomonas; bacterial sinusitis / OM → S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, S. aureus
  • Red flags: progressive sx, fever, ↓ neck ROM, trismus, prior abx; always consider the airway
  • Tonsillitis: peritonsillar swelling + uvula deviation → PTA → I&D; trismus + ↓ neck ROM → deep neck infection
  • Tonsillectomy (Paradise): 7 in 1 yr, 5/yr × 2 yr, 3/yr × 3 yr; also OSA, recurrent PTA, suspected malignancy
  • Epiglottitis (H. influenzae B, now uncommon): hot potato voice, tripod, drooling → secure airway, don't agitate
  • Diphtheria (C. diphtheriae): grey pharyngeal membrane + toxin myocarditis; unvaccinated
  • Deep neck space: oral flora → ceftriaxone + metronidazole; + vancomycin if MRSA colonized / PWID; + pip-tazo if immunocompromised / healthcare-associated; I&D ± steroids
  • Lemierre's = IJ septic thrombophlebitis, Fusobacterium necrophorum, after pharyngitis; CT with contrast; ceftriaxone + metronidazole; septic emboli
  • Rhinocerebral mucormycosis: DKA, immunocompromise, steroids, deferoxamine; rapid fever, sinus pain, headache → surgical debridement + liposomal amphotericin; very high mortality

lectures.framing: The oropharynx, middle ear, sinuses and eye are all connected, so an infection in one can spread to the others. The page is organised around which organisms live where (skin, mouth) and which do not belong (otitis externa, sinusitis/otitis media), because that decides the empiric antibiotic. It then covers tonsillitis, the common and once-common neck infections, and the rare ones: deep neck space infection, Lemierre's syndrome and mucormycosis.
lectures.keypoints: Skin flora: S. aureus and group A strep; oral flora: viridans strep + anaerobes. Otitis externa = Pseudomonas; sinusitis/otitis media = the pneumonia organisms (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis). Empiric H&N cover: ceftriaxone + metronidazole (or amox-clav); + vancomycin for MRSA risk, + pip-tazo only for Pseudomonas risk. Peritonsillar swelling + uvula deviation = peritonsillar abscess; trismus + ↓ neck ROM = deep neck infection. Paradise: 7 in 1 year, 5/yr for 2, 3/yr for 3. Lemierre's = Fusobacterium necrophorum IJV thrombophlebitis about a week after pharyngitis. Mucormycosis: necrotic palate in DKA or immunocompromise → amphotericin B + debridement.

lectures.name: Pediatric Neck Masses
lectures.title: Pediatric Neck Masses

blocks.html:
Approach to a child's neck mass
  • Hx: timing around infections (travel, TB, cat scratch); change in size with eating (salivary); growth (slow → benign, rapid → infection or malignancy); B symptoms (malignancy); changes with feeding and breathing
  • PEx
    • Node disease is rarely limited to the neck: check spleen, axilla, groin
    • Lymph nodes > 2 cm are not normal
    • Note the triangle (anterior vs posterior)
    • Consistency: firm → infection or malignancy; fluctuant → cyst or abscess; fixed → malignancy
  • Labs: CBC + diff, cat-scratch serology, tumour markers (VMA)
  • Imaging, simplest first: CXR (TB, sarcoidosis, malignancy) → ultrasound (solid vs cystic; limited for deep lesions) → CT with contrast (cellulitis vs abscess, relation to surrounding structures) → MRI (best soft tissue detail, often needs sedation)

rows: Lateral, along SCM; if unilateral usually right; 10% bilateral
Soft mass in the posterior triangle; H&N is the most common site
16% of pediatric neck masses; 70% of congenital cysts; the most common congenital neck mass
17% of masses; > 90% of branchial cleft anomalies; M = F
Thyroid starts at the foramen cecum and descends into the neck (done by week 7); cells left on the tract form the cyst
The 2nd arch overgrows the 3rd and 4th to fuse with the epicardial ridge in the lower neck; incomplete fusion leaves cysts and sinuses (1st cleft forms the external auditory meatus)
Vascular malformation of lymphatics (malformations can also be arterial or venous)
Around ages 3-5; elevates on tongue protrusion; enlarges or becomes infected after a URTI
80% by age 5; recurrent swelling with URTIs; recurrent discharge in the lower neck

Present at birth (60%), 90% by age 2; grows with the child; may change size; compressive symptoms (dysphagia, airway obstruction); prone to infection or trauma; fluctuant, lobulated, attached to skin but fixed to deep tissues

Ultrasound (superficial), CT (extent), MRI (multiplanar, best for nature and extent)
Macrocystic: spaces > 2 mL; microcystic: < 2 mL
DDx: hemangioma, solid tumour, ranula, other vascular malformation

Cystectomy alone: 20% recurrence
Sistrunk procedure (< 5%): cyst, thyroglossal tract, middle of the hyoid and base of tongue up to the foramen cecum; not during acute infection

Complete excision of sinus and tract: 3% recurrence
20% if previously drained or partially excised

Surgery is the treatment of choice: complete excision 10% recurrence vs incomplete 15-50%
Sclerotherapy (injected irritant scars the lumen); aspiration for symptoms; watch and wait (rarely resolves on its own)
blocks.lead: Congenital neck masses (> 50% of pediatric neck masses): present from birth, though they may not show until later

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• LN >2 cm → not typical in children
  • Labs: CBC + diff, cat-scratch serology, tumour markers (VMA)
  • TGDC: 70% of congenital cysts, midline, elevates on tongue protrusion, enlarges/infected after URI
  • TGDC Tx: Sistrunk = cyst + central hyoid + tract up to foramen cecum; not during acute infection
  • 2nd branchial cleft = >90% of BC anomalies; lateral, usually right if unilateral; recurrent swelling with URI, discharge in lower neck
  • BC Tx: complete excision of sinus + tract; prior drainage/partial excision → recurrence 3% → 20% (don't drain)
  • Lymphatic malformation: present at birth, grows with child; surgery = Tx of choice

lectures.framing: An adult neck mass is cancer until proven otherwise, but in children most neck masses are congenital (over 50%), then inflammatory, then neoplastic. The page covers the history, exam and imaging ladder for a child, then compares the three congenital lesions by where they sit (midline vs lateral), when they appear, and how surgery prevents recurrence.
lectures.keypoints: Thyroglossal duct cyst = midline, most common congenital neck mass (70% of congenital cysts), elevates on tongue protrusion, enlarges after a URTI; Sistrunk (cyst + tract + middle of hyoid) cuts recurrence from 20% to < 5%. Second branchial cleft cyst = lateral (> 90% of cleft anomalies), 80% by age 5, swells with URTIs, drains in the lower neck; complete excision (3% recurrence) and do not drain first (20%). Lymphatic malformation = posterior triangle, present at birth, grows with the child; 90% by age 2. Nodes > 2 cm are abnormal. Fluctuant = cyst/abscess; fixed = malignancy.

lectures.name: Pediatric Airway Pathology
lectures.title: Pediatric Airway Pathology

rows: Larger in proportion to the mouth
More anterior and superior (C4, descending to C6/7 with growth), which protects the airway
Cricoid cartilage: a complete ring that cannot expand to accommodate obstruction or ↑ airflow (adults are narrowest at the vocal folds)
blocks.lead: Pediatric vs adult upper airway

Stridor: a harsh sound from turbulent airflow through a narrowed airway. Causes: croup (most common), epiglottitis (less common since Hib vaccination but life-threatening); less likely foreign body, subglottic stenosis, subglottic hemangioma, vocal cord paralysis. Surgical airway: cricothyrotomy through the cricothyroid membrane; tracheostomy below the cricoid.

blocks.html:
Laryngotracheobronchitis (croup): subglottic obstruction
  • Most common cause of stridor; 3-5% of children get it
  • Viral: parainfluenza, RSV, influenza; spring and fall
  • Ages 6 months to 3 years
  • Low-grade fever, respiratory distress, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, barking cough, steeple sign on X-ray
  • Tx: hydration, cold humidification; steroids, nebulized epinephrine; intubation (rare)
Subglottic stenosis
  • Narrowing below the vocal cords; can follow endotracheal intubation when the tissue scars

Foreign body aspiration
  • History is most important, especially when the event was not witnessed
  • Most common at ages 1-3; boys > girls
  • Vegetable matter is the most common object (70-80%); if there is one foreign body, check for more
  • Lodges anywhere, most often the right main bronchus (wider and more vertical)
  • Ix: inspiratory/expiratory CXR (air trapping behind the obstruction); lateral decubitus films for uncooperative children
  • Rigid bronchoscopy if any one of: suggestive history, suggestive exam, CXR signs (air trapping)
  • Tx: retrieval in a controlled setting in the OR (laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy)

rows: Choking, gagging, paroxysms of coughing or airway obstruction at the moment of aspiration
The object lodges and reflexes fatigue; lasts hours to weeks; sometimes a wheeze.
blocks.lead: Three clinical phases of foreign body aspiration

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• DDx stridor: croup most common, epiglottitis; less likely FB, VC paralysis
  • Croup: parainfluenza/RSV/influenza, 6 mo-3 y, subglottic; low fever, inspiratory stridor, barking "seal" cough, steeple sign
  • Croup Tx: hydration, cold humidification; mod-severe → nebulized epi + steroids; intubation rare
  • FB: 1-3 y, boys, vegetable matter 70-80%; 3 phases acute (choking) → asymptomatic → complication
  • FB Ix: inspiratory/expiratory CXR; most often right mainstem; rigid bronchoscopy if any 1 of Hx / exam / imaging positive

lectures.framing: A child's airway is built differently from an adult's, and the differences explain why small amounts of swelling cause distress. The page starts with pediatric airway anatomy and what the type of stridor says about the level of obstruction, then covers the causes of pediatric stridor: croup (most common), epiglottitis, subglottic stenosis and foreign body aspiration.
lectures.keypoints: The pediatric airway is narrowest at the cricoid (a complete ring; adults are narrowest at the vocal folds). Inspiratory stridor = supraglottic/glottic, expiratory = lower airway, biphasic = subglottic. Croup = most common cause of stridor: parainfluenza, 6 months-3 years, barking cough, steeple sign; nebulized epinephrine + steroids. Foreign body: ages 1-3, boys, vegetable matter (70-80%), right main bronchus; history matters most; inspiratory/expiratory CXR shows air trapping; rigid bronchoscopy if any one of history, exam or imaging is positive. Subglottic stenosis follows intubation.
